lessons.title: User Input
objectives: read user input using the Scanner class
choose the right Scanner method for each input type
prompt the user before reading input

steps.code:
String favColor = readLine("Hello, what is your favorite color? ");
System.out.println(favColor);
steps.output: Hello, what is your favorite color? blue

points.text: Asks your question and hands back whatever the user typed, as text.
points.label: readLine

points.text: The question goes INSIDE the brackets. You don't print it separately.
points.label: the prompt

points.text: A box to keep the answer in, so you can use it later.
points.label: String favColor

points.text: The question and the answer end up on the same line, because the user types right where the cursor is.
points.label: one line

steps.instruction: Programs can ask the person using them a question.

steps.code:
String favColor = readLine("Hello, what is your favorite color? ");
System.out.println(favColor);
steps.after: The program waited, took the answer, and used it.
skills: read text from the user with readLine
steps.instruction: Run it. We'll type "blue" for you.

steps.code:
String favColor = readLine("Hello, what is your favorite color? ");
System.out.println(favColor);
steps.hint: Change the words inside the quotes.
steps.after: You decide exactly what it asks.
skills: read text from the user with readLine
steps.target: Hello, what is your favorite color? blue
steps.instruction: Change the question it asks. Run it.

points.text: Text — a name, a colour, a sentence. Gives back a String.
points.label: readLine

points.text: A whole number, like an age. Gives back an int, so you can do maths with it.
points.label: readInt

points.text: A decimal number, like a price or a distance. Gives back a double.
points.label: readDouble

points.text: true or false. Gives back a boolean.
points.label: readBoolean

points.text: All of them take the question as the thing in brackets.
points.label: all four

steps.instruction: There are four ways to read input, one per kind of answer.

steps.why: The name tells you what kind of answer it expects, and what type of box you need to store it in.
skills: choose between readLine, readInt, readDouble and readBoolean
steps.instruction: Match each one to what it reads.

steps.code:
int age = readInt("Hello, how old are you? ");
System.out.println(age + 1);

points.text: Gives back a real number, so age + 1 does maths and gives 17.
points.label: readInt

points.text: The box has to match what you asked for: a whole number goes in an int.
points.label: int age

points.text: You'd get the text "16", and age + 1 would glue instead of add.
points.label: if you used readLine

steps.instruction: Reading a number so you can calculate with it.

steps.why: The question stays on the same line as what they type. And because readInt gives a number, age + 1 is maths (17), not gluing (161).
steps.code:
int age = readInt("How old are you? ");
System.out.println("Next year: " + (age + 1));
opts: How old are you? Next year: 17

How old are you?

skills: choose between readLine, readInt, readDouble and readBoolean
steps.instruction: The user typed 16. What appears?

steps.code:
String name = readInt("What is your name? ");
System.out.println("Hi, " + name + "!");
steps.hint: A name is text, not a number. Which of the four reads text?
steps.after: The method has to match the kind of answer — and the box has to match the method.
skills: choose between readLine, readInt, readDouble and readBoolean
steps.target: What is your name? Hi, Ada!
steps.solution:
String name = readLine("What is your name? ");
System.out.println("Hi, " + name + "!");
steps.instruction: This asks for a name but reads it the wrong way. Fix it.

steps.hint: Miles can have a decimal, so use readDouble and store it in a double.
steps.after: Ask, store, use. That's every input program you'll write.
skills: use a value the user typed in your program
steps.target: How many miles have you traveled? 5.0
steps.solution:
double miles = readDouble("How many miles have you traveled? ");
System.out.println(miles * 2);
steps.instruction: Ask how many miles they travelled, then print it doubled.

lessons.title: Arithmetic Expressions
objectives: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations
predict the result of integer division
use the modulo operator to find remainders

points.text: Add, subtract, multiply. * is a star, not an ×.
Divide. It behaves differently for whole numbers than you expect — that's coming up.
Remainder. 7 % 2 is 1, because 2 goes into 7 three times with 1 left over.
Brackets, to force what happens first.

steps.instruction: Java does maths with these six symbols.

steps.after: Exactly like a calculator. The interesting part is next.
skills: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations
steps.instruction: Run it. Nothing surprising yet.

points.text: * and / and % happen BEFORE + and -. Same rule you already use in maths class.
points.label: first

points.text: 2 + 3 * 4 is 2 + 12, which is 14. It is NOT 5 * 4.
points.label: so

points.text: Put brackets around what you want to happen first.
points.label: override

steps.instruction: When there's more than one operator, order matters.

steps.why: Brackets go first, so it's 5 * 4 = 20. Without them it would have been 14.
skills: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations
steps.instruction: Brackets added. Now what?

points.text: When BOTH numbers are whole numbers, Java throws away the fraction. It does not round.
points.label: 3, not 3.5

points.text: A whole number divided by a whole number has to stay a whole number. 3.5 can't fit, so the .5 is dropped.
points.label: why

points.text: Gives 4, not 4.5 and not 5. Always chops downward.
Make one of them a decimal: 7.0 / 2 gives 3.5.
points.label: want 3.5?

steps.instruction: Now the one that catches everybody.

steps.why: Both are whole numbers, so the .5 is thrown away and you get 4.
skills: predict the result of integer division
steps.instruction: So what does this print?

steps.why: The division happens FIRST, as whole numbers, giving 4. Only then is 4 stored in a double. Storing it in a double afterwards can't bring the .5 back — it prints 4.0.
skills: predict the result of integer division
steps.instruction: This one looks safe but isn't. Tap the line that goes wrong.

steps.hint: One of the two numbers has to be a decimal BEFORE the division happens.
steps.after: Making one side a decimal changes the whole sum to decimal maths.
skills: predict the result of integer division
steps.instruction: Make it print the real average, 4.5.

points.text: 2 fits into 7 three times (6), and 1 is left over. So 1.
5 fits exactly, nothing left over. So 0.
A remainder of 0 means it divides evenly — that's how you test if a number is even, or a multiple of anything.
points.label: 0 means

steps.instruction: % gives you what's left over.

skills: use the modulo operator to find remainders

questions.why: 4 fits exactly 5 times, nothing left over.

steps.instruction: Work these out.

steps.hint: Even means: divide by 2 and nothing is left over.
steps.after: n % 2 == 0 is the standard way to test for even. You'll use it constantly.
skills: use the modulo operator to find remainders
steps.instruction: Fill it in so it only prints when n is even.

steps.hint: Use the same n % 2 == 0 test, with an else for the other case.
